utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Dr. Karadzic, if you would like to commence your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good morning, everyone, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before I begin my cross-examination, I would like to tell you that I would rather not conduct it at all because of my feelings of solidarity for you because of all the horrors that you lived through, and I would kindly ask you to clarify the circumstances in Grbavica during those months rather than deal with the horrific events that you yourself experienced. So I would kindly ask you to work together with me so that we can see exactly what was happening. In your amalgamated statement, paragraph 7, you describe the confiscation or seizure of cars committed by young men with masks on their heads. How long did this last, this confiscation of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talked about masks on the heads, what I meant was the date, the 1st to the 2nd of March night, and what I saw in the media. That was the first thing, because this happened immediately close to the place where I lived. However, this continued later in a period. I cannot establish it precisely, but I looked from my window as they were stopping cars, standing on the street. And under threat of weapons, they would get the person out of the car, then they would get in the car. The person would be left behind just looking at them. They would drive off quickly. I saw that. I used to see that, not once but a number of times. And first of all, I was thinking how is this possible? How can I be seeing this at all? This went on for days, let's say. I can't really specify exactly. I mean, it wouldn't be fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I understand you correctly that it wasn't necessarily night, that they did this in daylight as well?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. What I'm saying that I saw happened in daylight. The first time I saw it, though, it happened at night, because we were woken up by these voices. We live on the high -- ground floor, and you could hear -- I mean, the windowpanes were broken in this room where we were sleeping, so we improvised something, but it felt like we were directly on the street. These voices woke me up and I could see and hear something. This is speaking about the events that happened at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I need to wait for the translation because we speak the same language. Was it possible to see roughly the age of these masked persons?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that they were younger men. I could conclude that by their gestures, by their behaviour, by the way they looked. They looked like younger people in their 20s, 30s. Twenty-five to 30, perhaps a little bit older, but in any case, younger people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In April were there any policemen on the street to whom those people whose cars were seized could complain?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't any. This happened so quickly that one couldn't possibly react in any other way than just to be left standing on the street. I remember one gentleman who came out. He was holding some kind of overcoat in his hand and he was waiting. Perhaps he thought it was some kind of inspection or something, a flash inspection that was going to pass, but he was turned out of his car so quickly that he just stood like that, and as he was looking, they already drove away. You could see that they were driving away towards Vraca, the intersection towards Vraca, leading from Zagrebacka Street towards Vraca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I don't want to stay on this topic too long, but can you just tell us whether you had any information that the cars were taken to a specific place or could their owners see them around later? You don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It would be ridiculous to conclude that they could look for the car because of the things that followed after that. I mean, it just wasn't realistic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 22 of your amalgamated statement you say that Serbs and Muslims were leaving Grbavica in large numbers at that time while it was still possible to leave Grbavica. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that. There was no rule, which is why I said that people were leaving. Some took more things with them, some took less, depending on what they expected. I could perhaps say what they maybe knew, what they assumed would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to say until when it was possible to leave without any organised way of crossing over or asking for some particular permission or paper? For how long was it possible to leave Grbavica just like that and come back?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you about my own case specifically. On the 27th of May -- actually, on the 26th of May, I tried to cross over together with my sister, because her family had crossed over to the other side, crossing over the Brotherhood and Unity Bridge. They went to their cousins. We tried to cross at the same place. We still had some food in the house, and we wanted to carry all of that across for her children, because the most important thing was for them not to feel any shortages. It wasn't much, but whatever you would usually find in a house. We tried that day. We didn't succeed because there were guards all over the place. We were stopped. They asked us where we were going. We explained that we wanted to cross over. They said you can't do that, so we gave up that day, and then the following day, on the 27th, we tried again, and then we were fortunate and did cross over. We passed through an inspection. The person was asking us -- there was some shops close by. Everything was open, everything was being taken out. You could see everything. You just kind of register that, but you try more not to notice than to notice. And somehow we managed to reach the bridge. It was a small pedestrian bridge leading towards the Hotel Bristol, and we did cross over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. When you say "taken out," things were being taken out, are you saying that they were being robbed or things were being bought?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was looting and robbery. Glass was broken. There was packaging, shoe boxes, all kinds of stuff that were left over just strewn about. It was a small area, and the buildings were very close together, so all these other shops and facilities were also close together, and they were there at the same place at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, but I'm just wondering if Madam Witness could be cautioned to make a small pause before she answers to allow for our colleagues to catch up in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It's easily --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, no need to apologise because you're not used to it, and it's easily done. Where both the questioner and the person being questioned speak the same language, it's natural that you have a conversation, and exceptional though our interpreters are, they can't work magic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You returned on the same day?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we returned the same day. I can't really say what time it was, but judging by the panic in town, we could see that something was happening, but since we were in a part of town where the telephones were not working, I'm talking about Ciglana, on our way back we met a colleague of mine from work who asked me what's happening with me, where I was, and I explained and he said, Where are you going now? And I said I'm going back home. He asked me am I crazy. Do I know? Did I know what happened today? I really didn't know and then when we came to the Kosevo Street leading towards the Presidency building, we saw horrific images. I will find it very difficult to forget them. There were different cars, vehicles, ambulances, private cars rushing towards the hospital. The sirens were on. Later we found out that a shell had struck and that the massacre happened in which two of my professors were killed. Perhaps there was some confusion there. One professor, I apologise, was actually wounded, Milan Banjac, and the other professor, who used to teach mathematics to me, he was killed. And we came back. It took a while. We had to run across pedestrian crossings, jump over things. There was some improvised shelters to protect us from fire. We were running across. My sister was a little bit -- well, I had a problem. I was always a bit braver. I had to keep encouraging her, going back for her. Then we reached the small bridge, and we crossed over that same bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And your sister, she definitely left with her family; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My sister actually followed after her family, which was already at Ciglana, like I said before. My mother was a big problem for me, and if I regret anything, it's that I never -- I didn't leave Grbavica, but I couldn't prevail on my mother who didn't want to leave. She believed that all these things wouldn't happen. And that day when we came back, perhaps I wouldn't have even come back, and the reason why I came back was actually that we couldn't get in touch with her by phone. Phones where we were were still operating till June. So my sister and I couldn't get in touch with my mother on the phone. I could imagine that she was worried. She could have assumed that we were in some bread line. I mean, it would be easy to imagine that we had gone to buy something. And this is why I returned and I stayed with my mother after my sister left, which actually turned out to be quite dramatic as she told us later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would kindly ask you to answer more succinctly, and I will try to put my questions more briefly as well. I read somewhere in your statements that already at that time in Grbavica you were not getting bread from the federal part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a situation that I described. Bread would arrive in front of the Mis. Those from Grbavica would know that that is on the intersection leading towards Vraca. The bread would be delivered there. We would wait in line. We would take the bread. So I'm already talking about the period of June, after the 11th of June. Until then it was possible to take -- to get bread -- I mean, there were some armed people standing there, but if there was enough bread, you felt lucky you would get it. If not, then you would have to find another way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how many times did you personally leave Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in that period?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time I left Grbavica was on the 25th [as interpreted] of May, and then when I came back I didn't leave anymore. I did try sometime in June, but I didn't go farther than Soping. I didn't get farther than the military command or something.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the transcript please change, the witness said the 27th and it says the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can see in your statements, then, you tried on a number of occasions to leave Grbavica and that this was not possible. Can you briefly tell us what was the procedure after mid-June when somebody wanted to leave Grbavica? Do you remember that it was necessary for somebody to put you on a list, somebody from the federal part, to put you on the list? And generally, how was it done that you could cross in buses over the Brotherhood and Unity Bridge?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot talk about the federal part. I can only speak about myself. I didn't have a telephone, because it was physically removed. Even the telephone sets were broken. Therefore, I had no possibility to get in touch with anyone. There was a young neighbour of mine, a young girl, who immediately after she'd left Grbavica got killed by a shell. She came to our place because she had heard what my mother and I had gone through, and she said if we wanted to be put on a list that would then be sent to the command, because that was the procedure, she said that all you need to give me is your ID card. I said, "Amila, we don't have our ID cards and I can't do that."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But did you ever find out that at certain periods there were some rounds of groups of Muslims going from Grbavica to the federal part and the Serbs coming into Grbavica, that all of that was conducted across the Brotherhood and Unity Bridge?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when was this happening?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was later when one registered first and then required a permit, and we were allowed to even bring some of our belongings with us, but that was later. I think it was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us in more detail what kind of an insignia were worn by these armed young men? What did they have on their caps? Let's start with that.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about different periods. There were cockades. There were caps with five-pointed stars at the beginning, which looked a bit ridiculous, because I had always had a good opinion about the Yugoslav Army. And then they started wearing patches on their jackets, which was a circular one with the inscription "The Army of Republika Srpska," and a flag. And we also had a sticker with this insignia attached to our door to indicate that our flat had been inspected by the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did that mean that there was no additional inspection required?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I thought too. However, our neighbours told us that we need to put our name on the door, because it was known that there were Muslims there, because somebody was regularly reporting the situation. So we had to put our family name on the door, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These weekend searches, who were the people who did that? What did they wear, and what kind of insignia did they have?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I am referring to soldiers in uniform, because there were several instances. I can't tell you exactly the number of times it happened and was repeated. The upper part was a uniform, and the lower part of the outfit was the civilian clothes. Two men would come, invariably, each time, and over and over again you go through the same fear. You can't explain things, and on the other hand, you must try and act as normally as possible in order for them not to realise that you were actually afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any parts of Grbavica where it was unsafe to go through, people had to run across, and do you remember if blankets were put in the streets as a kind of barrier?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that happened a little bit later, because I wasn't going out much in that initial period. A wall was even built in front of our house overnight, it was a pretty high wall, a little bit higher than the average height of a person, on the grounds that fire was coming from Debelo Brdo and that protection was needed. Although, if I'm being honest, no incident happened there. At least I didn't see or hear anything happening at that particular spot. There were those blankets hanging along this route, and I'm talking about Grbavicka Street, which is opposite Vilsonovo Setaliste. They were erected on several places, but I'm talking about the nearest one that I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These searches that you mentioned in your statements took place more often than not over a weekend. Did the same people always came, or did different people come to conduct these searches?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Different people came. I remember that from the previous group or of the two, if there were two, I would recognise only one. They would go from flat to flat. They would start with our flat and then move onwards and upwards. After that, our neighbours said that since the front door was completely demolished and unhinged, that we should put something to close the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the -- the entrance door?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm talking about flats, because flats were forcibly opened if they were empty, and there were quite a few flats in our apartment building. There were 16 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And many people had left.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Those who came to search the flats did not wear any masks?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are talking about how you went to the cellar where you could find shelter during shelling.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was part of subterranean part of the building, because it had windows almost of the same size as the ones that we had. Therefore, they were so big that you couldn't feel safe at all, but we thought that that was at least a little bit safer than our flats. That was a flat that belonged to a neighbour of ours who had left. So it was not exactly an abandoned place. It was simply a place where you can spend some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How often did you go to this shelter?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the day we might have gone once, although I already started feeling certain of anxiety and awkwardness. I -- it was kind of looks that we received and the questions that were asked of us in terms of why hadn't we crossed over, what were we doing there. It sounded as if they were concerned, but in most cases that was actually a message: Go away so that we don't have problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are talking about your neighbours who also used this same shelter.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far or how close did the shells land in order for you to go to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They fell rather close. There were a couple of situations when after we had made some makeshift -- or took the windows from the next room and put it in the living-room another shell will -- would break those windows again. Now, what I'm talking about is what happened in the close proximity to the building where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was anyone killed close to your flat or your street in those days?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that a young girl was killed at the very beginning, and I think she lived in the neighbouring apartment building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did it come from Debelo Brdo? Where did it come?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you that. There was, for example, a car that was parked nearby. There were pieces of metal. Although, I personally did not see the place where the shell landed. I only see the effects, and they were obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraphs 82 through to 91, you describe how, on the 1st of October in 1992, a soldier forced you to give the key to your flat that was subsequently sealed. Then the military police explained to you that that kind of behaviour was illegal and that it was not based on any order.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't say that in so many words. They only said that this operation was aborted. I even told them that this soldier introduced himself as Simic. Later I found out that he was from Zavidovici. They said that this operation was suspended and that no one was to leave Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't know to which unit this Simic man belonged?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no, no, no. He would introduce himself by putting his hand on his handgun and telling me that I have to go out with him in order for the flat to be searched. That is something that caused a personal distress for me, because it was night-time. There was no electricity. We had a couple of candles. And this is where I stood and talked with him. He said he wanted to search the flat and that for that purpose he needed the key. I put the key in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Simic came by himself on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Simic came by himself, and he said specifically, "I have a tip-off," and for quite some time later I had this fear, because he had a piece of paper with our names on it, and he said that he had received a tip-off about a mother and a daughter living there. And every time, whenever I saw anyone holding a piece of paper similar to that one, it would take me some time to compose myself. So he went to our flat once. He came out shortly afterwards. My mother was not feeling well. We were busy taking care of her. However, he told me that I should accompany him into my flat, allegedly to show him where everything was. I don't know. It was pitch dark. I think that we didn't even have a candle. We just had some improvised things. Even that was running out, this material that we sort of improvised lighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that electricity was cut off quite often.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally the power supply was cut off, and one had to adapt to such situations and try somehow to survive the period without electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraphs -- or in paragraph 40 of your amalgamated statement, you say that in early June 1992, you saw the perpetrator of the crime against you for the first time, and his name was Veselin Vlahovic, aka Batko.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not June, July. July 1992. I can briefly describe this situation. I was in a flat of a neighbour of mine who had invited me for some reason. They had electricity. The atmosphere there was kind of normal. They were watching TV, and they offered me to sit down, and then at one point, of course not knowing that I was going to see that, while watching TV I saw this person, and I started crying out loud. They didn't know what was going on. I didn't tell them anything, but I think that I said something, "Wow, it's him." They didn't press me with any questions, but they did realise that something was going on. So what I saw was this footage, and what -- what horrified me was that this Veselin Vlahovic was actually standing in front of our building. I'm talking about this footage. And there was a tank. He was standing next to it. So as soon as you leave the building, that was the place that you can see with the naked eye. This is where he was standing and making a statement to a SRNA journalist, reporter. Whether the Muslims were coming back to Grbavica again, that was the question, and his answer was, The Balijas would never live in Grbavica again. So that was the first time that I saw this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was the first time that you identified him. You didn't know his name before?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this happened to us, a female neighbour of ours would occasionally bring us bread, because that was our major problem. Everything else was a problem, but of course without bread, you can't do anything. On the 28th of June, that same person took her away, but something prevented him from taking her away while his car was still running, and he parked his car in a different place, and by some kind of miracle she avoided being taken by this same man. Before that, we were conversing, and there was already mention that this person was known as a Batko. There were stories circulating around Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, on page 13194, I'm giving the page reference so that the other participants can find this, you confirmed that this man belonged to an organised military group. He came to see you by himself when he committed these crimes; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time he came with another soldier. He asked for our personal IDs. He gave certain comments with regards to what our IDs contained: My age, what I looked like, things like that. The other man didn't do anything. That was our first encounter with him. And the second time he came was during that night, after the police had come to see us. The next day the military police came. I'm saying that because of those white belts, and I had some relatives who belonged to such units, so -- I mean in peacetime, had belonged to these units in peacetime. So I could recognise the military police therefore. So everybody addressed the commander of that unit as Zenga, Zenga. Zenga. So I have to say that he was very polite at the very outset. He addressed us in a very polite way. He asked for our IDs, and he was saying that we were just sitting there while his people were getting killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's the one who had a Croatian accent; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was my impression, yes. I think that that was the case. He sounded like someone who had lived in Croatia a long time. You can hear that kind of accent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Zenga was the abbreviation used for members of Tudjman's National Guards Corps? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on I knew about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So your impression was that he was threatening to use some group of Chetniks. Again I'm talking about the perpetrator of the crime, that he was relying on someone. Did that lead you to say that he was part of a group?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. I think he was a member of the army, the regular army. The others who came with him -- well, perhaps when you're afraid you seem to see things bigger than they are, but they were very tall men, the ones who came with him. One stayed in front of a door that was open, and he stood there with a rifle sort of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about Zenga now, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I thought that we should go back to Batko.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have the impression that he was threatening you with some group of his, and did that lead you to believe that he had an organised group?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. That was not his comment. I said that he was talking about what I looked like, and he asked me whether that was my personal ID and whether I was that age, and I said of course. That was the comment. And then like whether there were any searches, or not, no, no. He wasn't hinting at anything then, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But later on in your statements, you say that he threatened you, that he would hand you over to the Chetniks or something like that.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was when he took us away during the night. That night and the next day, I can't remember exactly -- I cannot actually assess the time-frame. He kept us at this apartment in Vraca in Petrovacka Street. Excuse me. I started reacting when he mentioned that he would execute my mother by some brook and hand me over to his Chetniks. He kept using derogatory terms all the time, terrible insults, and his beating was merciless. I cannot say that I'm very frail exactly, but it's not that I'm that sturdily built either. It was terrible, all of it. Seeing my mother lying there next to me. I actually just started reacting when he said he would do that. He also mentioned a brothel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned some strange behaviour on his part, grabbing his head. You're referring to headaches, confusing behaviour, confused behaviour. Can you tell us what this was all about?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in some apartment, and the two of us were definitely shocked there. The doors -- the windows were open in that apartment. Things were strewn about, and at one point my mother tripped over. He climbed up on this open window, and he sat there. And I see the silhouette now as I'm saying this. It was night-time, and then he said, "No, no. Not there. Let's move on." And now I'm in an area that I'm totally unfamiliar with. My mother tripped over at one point, and she said that her shoe fell off, and I kept encouraging her, "Mama, take it easy. I'll do it." And I bent over to get her shoe, and we stepped on a body. That's a terrible feeling. At that moment I see -- I mean, what can I expect. And we came to this other apartment where there was electricity, and let us say that that was the living-room of that apartment. And on a table I see jewellery, money. Everything seems -- well, he is sort of looking for a pill or something. He has a headache. He's holding his head. And at one point he walks into another room. I look at my mother. I think she understood me, and I'm walking towards the window. And I say to her, "Mama, I'm going to jump out of the window." And she just looks at me, and I don't see any sign of approval there, in her look, nothing. And I see bars on the window, and at that moment he is hollering at me, saying, "Where are you going?" And I just sat by my mother then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's the part that I was interested in the most. In your statements you say that he behaved like a madman.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, he's holding his head, and, you know, the way he's driving and everything. I don't know. I seem to have come to now. But in that moment, he was holding his head and looking for a pill, a pain-killer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, in your statement of the 17th of February, 1996, or it's probably the 21st as you said yesterday, you describe him as a member of the Serb army without all of these details, but yesterday you mentioned that he wore a former JNA uniform without any insignia. Can you tell us actually what he looked like, whether he was tidy and what his general condition was?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I first saw was his overcoat. He wore a military uniform, full military uniform, but he had this overcoat. That's why I had that impression. He therefore looked sort of untidy, because it was the wrong size. It was too big for him. By the next day he was wearing camouflage uniform, just a blouse and trousers. But if you're asking about later on, I saw him through the window of our apartment. Again -- well, all of a sudden he was wearing something like overalls and then a military jacket over it. I mean, well, he changed uniforms all the time. Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm a bit perplexed by the jewellery. At one point you say that it was in a jar and in another statement you say that it was on the table.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no, no. I was probably referring to the jewellery that we had hidden in our own apartment and not in a jar but in a pillow, and it was sewed up. Over here it was very obvious. I saw it right in front of me. I sat on a sofa, and in front of me on a table there was lots of jewellery, thick chains. It was very, very obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript, line 6, page 20, the witness said that later she saw him in a third type of clothing. I guess that we were speaking very fast and perhaps you didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was your impression that he was in these two apartments and that this other apartment was where he kept -- kept most of his valuables.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first apartment was not really very well equipped with any kind of amenities, but the second one, I told you what it looked like, the one where we spent the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm really unhappy to deal with this scene, but I would like us to draw a distinction in relation to your statements. In one statement you say that when this occurred your mother was in another room, but in other statement you say that just before the act occurred, he brought your mother in.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We were together in this living-room, if we can call it that, and then he beat my mother and threatened her and took her away. I didn't even know what the layout of the apartment looked like at that point in time. He took her away. He took her somewhere. I have to put it that way, "somewhere." I hear her cries and moaning. She is begging him not to tie her up. She says that she is in pain, and she even says, "I could be your mother." After that, he returned. My mother stayed then. However, since this went on during the entire night, you're probably talking about what followed. I know that the best. Of course, later on he did bring my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. It's the first statement of the 17th of February, page 4, around line 15. All right. But basically, it doesn't change much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have a look at document 1D3415. Can we have that in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again, I would like to recall that you said that he belonged to some organised military group. May I draw your attention to this. This was taken off the official site of the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The second paragraph, the first line: "The indictment alleges, inter alia, that the accused Vlahovic, as a member of the paramilitary forces of the so-called Serb Republic of BiH, later Republika Srpska, persecuted the civilian non-Serb population from Grbavica, Vraca and Kovacici settlements." That what you meant when you said he belonged to some organised group?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have a problem with the characterisation of this question, Your Honour. The -- this report on the confirmation of the indictment refers to -- or uses the word "paramilitary forces" to describe the organised forces of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I don't think that's an appropriate question in any case for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, it's certainly not something that I anticipate the witness would have any direct knowledge of. This was a question of a form of art by the person who drafted the indictment. I very much doubt, Dr. Karadzic, that this line of questioning is really going to assist. The question that I anticipate you were posing really should be put towards the person, whoever that might have been, who drafted this indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we briefly have a look at two other documents, 1D3414. 1D3414.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This man is confessing his crimes and is not repenting at all. Does this look like him?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of him being called the "Monster of Grbavica"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to find an appropriate term, but this one is most suitable.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, the -- are you asking that it's admitted as evidence of the truth of its contents or simply for the accuracy of the description of the perpetrator as being a monster?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And what is particularly horrifying here for me is the absence of repentance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I may say this: He's not the first one. A soldier monster, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, what do you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's just another characterisation of the first point that I rose on, Your Honour: What's a paramilitary, in effect? No. I don't think there's any basis for admission of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that's why I posed the question that I did. It seems to me that the witness has already answered that calling him a monster is an accurate description, and that's already in evidence in the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So I think it's safer to leave it at that, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 1D3417 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, is it correct that this person was arrested in Spain and that now he's facing trial in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand whether that's correct or not. It is that same man. The years have passed, and he, like everyone else, like all of us, looks different because of the years that have gone by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you because of the other parties to the proceedings. They don't have to know what we know from the media.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The lawyer of this person here notes that -- I'm going to read that in English. Second paragraph: "[In English] Radivoje Lazarevic, the Defence attorney for suspect Vlahovic, says he expects the indictment to be filed 'in a few days' because the investigation began 'more than two and a half years ago.'" [No interpretation]. "[In English] 'Vlahovic approached me several times, complaining about various problems he has, most of which are related to his mental health. I advised him to visit a physician at the Detention Unit. I even think he visited him twice and some symptoms were found,' said -- Lazarevic said." [Interpretation] Does this description of him by his lawyer correspond to your impression when you went to this other apartment when he was holding his head and all of that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. I'm not that kind of expert. What is being talked about here is what was done and the passage of time. If that person, after what he had done, is able to have peace of mind and sleep peacefully, that would be something strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statements you mentioned who was on the other side of the river, on the other bank. Is it correct that the HVO component of the B and H Army was located there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that when we crossed the small bridge, a soldier who was checking our IDs - I'm talking about the 27th of May - commented the origin of my family and he mentioned her mother, who is from Herzegovina, let's say, and I think he did say this was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The time that was allocated for cross-examination has actually expired five minutes ago, but we are minded to grant some extra time bearing in mind that since that allocation was assessed, there was an additional material, some additional material, but we'd ask you, please, to aim to finish your cross-examination by 20 past 10.00 -- just one moment. Ms. Edgerton, how much time would you anticipate, if any, for redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The ten minutes after that would do it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you now tell us how the supermarket that you saw was destroyed, demolished, the one that you saw in ruins, and how was it looted?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was torched. The fire spread to our building as well. Actually, the smoke caught our building as well. There was a warehouse there, so we ourselves tried to extinguish the fire. The people who lived in neighbouring apartments all around me, we tried to extinguish the fire on the roof of the supermarket.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you were a part of the Civilian Defence. Did you do this fire-fighting as part of the fire-fighting civil protection unit, or did you do it as volunteers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We just came out of our apartments. We were in a panic, and we took whatever we had, filled buckets with water, whatever we could find and we were pouring this water from above on the roof of this supermarket to stop the fire from spreading. It wasn't organised at all. I came out in my housecoat.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the witness has never said she was part of the civilian defence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. With that correction, Dr. Karadzic, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were you subject to work duty? I perhaps mixed it up, but I think you mentioned both.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you probably did mix it up. I was not subject to work duty, but I was in the work platoon that was formed in Grbavica and which, from time to time, went to the military farm in Gornja Presjenica. We went to Kijevo. I think that's what those places were called where we would go from time to time, and we would cultivate crops. We would dig up onions, potatoes, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And that is where your got two meals; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depending on the time we spent there, yes, we did. We did get a meal. All right. It was a meal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you described some people who were carrying some kind of scabbards or holsters. Did you see anybody fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I went out every day, every day I would see certain people. There weren't too many of them, not too many familiar faces to me at least. I could see them entering the entrance at Lenjinova 58. Later that became the street of Nikola Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I can see that I found somewhere in your statement the Women's Organisation of Women Victims of War of the 27th of January, 2006, page 046757569, paragraph 5, where you -- paragraph 4, where you say that you and your mother were -- received notice to go to the civil protection, that you were summoned to go to the civilian protection just as the women of all ethnic groups were summoned to work. It wasn't work on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a wrong translation. It was not civil protection but it was the work platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now that is clear to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just give me a moment, please. I'm asking for a little bit of patience because I have to skip some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This Batko introduced himself falsely. In your amalgamated statement, in paragraph 58, you say that he said that you could call him Dragan.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. That's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't expect him to tell me his full first and last name or to show any kind of consideration or respect for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that he himself was aware what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I cannot say that. Perhaps you know that in view of your profession, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in any case, he had the need to conceal his identity; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that kind of thing, you know how it was. He said, "You can call me Dragan," even though no one asked him anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 88, you say that these military policemen -- this military policeman sat you down and explained to you, when you asked them to let you go or to kill you, he explained, he sat you down and explained to you, "We don't that." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It was ironic, but it was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You asked him to "expel us [In English] at least to the smaller bridge, and they said that wasn't being done any longer and that Grbavica was completely sealed. They said that what happened yesterday had been stopped." [Interpretation] Here you say that some people were expelled the previous day.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Right. I was in a hopeless situation. I didn't have a flat. I didn't have any documents. There was nowhere I could go and seek shelter. I didn't know what to do. And I said that in desperation, in pleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that topic doesn't touch me very much, but you mentioned this Mr. Aleksic. Yes, he really does look unconventional. However, you don't know of any of his criminal acts, do you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that visit of Seselj's that we looked at here? Do you recall that in mid-May, a referendum was held in Republika Srpska on the Vance-Owen Plan and that he mentions voting and the fact that 60 Muslims voted in Grbavica in that excerpt? Do you agree that that visit of Seselj's was in connection to the referendum?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't say that. All I know is that I did not participate in the referendum. Without an ID card you absolutely are nobody and nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that on this market it was possible to buy and that there was a certain degree of supplies?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some products. More homemade ones. It was quite meager. Some agriculture products, something from humanitarian aid. Actually, it was a very, very meager offering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to touch on any other topics. Just one question: Did you hear of any names of any paramilitary groups? For example, did you hear of the Beli Andjeli, White Angels, paramilitary group?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps later. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the White Eagles, Beli Orlovi, or some other one, Emperor Dusan, Tsar Dusan?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps the White Eagles, Beli Orlovi. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we going to admit this 15 -- 13417, 13417 that was shown last?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I don't think the witness was able to speak to that document at all, so it falls into the category of documents which you might seek to have admitted through another method later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, I am deeply grateful to you, and I am completely in solidarity with you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to pause a little bit at these words. Thank you, Mr. Accused, for that understanding of yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Madam Witness, today at page 11, line 23, through to page 12, line 12, you discussed with Dr. Karadzic a period of time during which you went to the cellar of your building to find shelter during the shellings, and that's referred to in your amalgamated statement at paragraph 12. Was this limited to any particular period of time where you went to the cellar to find shelter during the shellings?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did go, just like everybody else did, and then as the days went by, we went more and more seldom, because we didn't feel comfortable. I said that. Namely, our neighbours were listening to Radio Belgrade, and I was supposed to listen to what Belgrade was saying that was happening to us. I couldn't accept that, because these were pure untruths. I can believe that people really -- when the same things are constantly being repeated people start to believe them. Some people; not me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What period of time was that limited to?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean when we went down to the shelter? Well, if not every day, then there was a period, and I'm referring to the day when I was -- we were taken away, we were in the shelter. However, immediately before that, we went up to our flat because I was very hungry. Our neighbours who had rifles could hear what was happening, that somebody had come, that they were pulling us out. My mother was screaming calling the names of our neighbours, Radoslav Vuckovic among them. However, everybody kept quiet. Nobody helped us in any way whatsoever. I'm talking about those who had rifles. I'm not talking about the civilians. I understand that everybody is afraid and trying to save their own skin, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I take from your answer, then, this period where you would seek shelter is limited to this very beginning period of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exclusively, even though it might sound as leading, but, you know, after you experience certain things, then you move to another level of struggle to survive, not in a shelter any longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, at page 13 of today's transcript, with respect to events on October 1st, 1992, Dr. Karadzic put the following to you, he said: "Then the military police explained to you that that kind of behaviour was illegal and that it was not based on any order." But then later in today's transcript he referred to your statement at paragraph 88 and read the following: "I asked them again to expel us, at least to the smaller bridge. They said that wasn't being done any longer and that Grbavica was completely blocked. They said what had happened yesterday had been stopped." Could you tell us, then, which is correct or a correct rendering of events, what Dr. Karadzic put to you or what he read to you at paragraph 88 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact word of the military policeman, Boro Sljuka, because I saw his name tag, was that that operation was suspended. These things were not being done any longer. Grbavica was under blockade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now finally at page 19, lines 13 to 14, Dr. Karadzic told you that in your statements you said that, referring to Batko, he behaved like a madman. Have you ever -- do you recall every using the word "madman" to describe Batko?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never said that, because I tried to avoid using such qualifications. I'll leave that to the gentleman who is a psychiatrist by vocation. Only at that moment when he put his hands on his head, I think that, in inverted commas, this people -- this man who was "insane," came to our door. He wanted to return our ID cards. He was banging at our door so fiercely that I think that he was going to break into. I had no other choice but to open the door. Of course, he had no ID cards of ours with him, and all these horrible events then followed. The whole of that night and the following day. But this is how it started. He pushed us -- pushed us into a cart -- a car. I think it was a Golf one. He forced us. I had problems with my mother. He was driving fast. He knew exactly where he was. Everything was being done by design. Nobody asked me this, but if I may say, when I reacted for the first time, when I felt that I might perhaps survive, I was affected much more about -- by what he said, that he was going to shoot my mother dead and then take me to a brothel and hand me over to Chetniks. At that point I started thinking very intensively, because although everything was going according to his plan, he asked me, and I think it is in one of my statements, "Have you got anything to buy your lives with?" I just waited to see what he was referring to, and he said, "Do you have money?" I said, "A little." Then he asked, "Do you have gold?" And I immediately said, "Yes, we do." He asked then, "Plenty of gold?" I said, "Yes." And then he said, "If you trick me, I'm going to kill you in front of your mother." From that moment on, I tried to continue living just for us to leave that place and, before that, to give him whatever he wanted and he thought sufficient. After that, he changed his uniform. He looked a completely different person. He was in a camouflage uniform. We went back again in this same Golf, entered the flat, and we started looking for this pillow in panic, given that a search had been conducted by the military police before and everything was ransacked. All the things that were in cupboards were thrown onto the floor. So it took some time for us to find this pillow where my mother had hidden gold. He took these two pouches, and before that he had threatened us by saying, "If you are lying to me," he also fired some bullets close to my head, "I am going to kill you in front of your mother." However, as soon as he saw this gold, he took it and said, "If you decide to go out, if you talk to anyone about this, I have my men. I have my snipers. I have my men who are going to kill you." And then he left.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give evidence before us. It has not been contested that you have -- but that you have gone through a dreadful personal ordeal, and you are obviously a very strong lady. Good fortune for the future, and a safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I am grateful for having this opportunity, although this is terrible for me to testify, nevertheless, in this case and to give my account of what really was actually the point where my normal life stopped. There have been some improvements, but this is my personal thing. And also on behalf of my mother, I would like to thank you, because she's not capable of giving testimony. This is what I owe to her. And I also did this for all those who were killed in Grbavica. Some of them were found. Some have still not been found. So I'm thanking you on behalf of the living and the dead. Everyone says that I am a brave and patient woman, and I'm going to wait for justice with patience, and it might come eventually. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: We'll rise now until 11.00. Madam, if you stay seated until the curtains are lowered and then leave when it's safe for you to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you for returning to continue with your testimony. I'm sorry about the length of the delay. Now we will continue. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, let me remind you where we were when we adjourned the other day. There was discussion about your comments at the 17th Assembly session, that is the 17th session of the Republika Srpska Assembly in July of 1992, and we were looking at comments in which you were discussing a meeting in Ilidza with Mr. Karadzic and others that you say took place on the 18th of April, 1992. And as I'm sure you'll recall, there was discussion about a particular word in the text. I don't know that there's any particular value in pursuing that discussion further. The Court will have the text in front of it. I think you've made your points about the text. You've mentioned, for example, the word "potisli" instead of the word "potjerali." But I noted that you had said toward the end of your testimony the very last thing you said: "If this is an original, then I accept it, and I am interpreting it. I can indicate another word that is important in order to interpret what you're asking me and it's a little different." So before we move on, I will give you an opportunity to say if you want to suggest another word instead of the word that appears in the text, and remind you that you have already said that you said "potisli," that is that your position is the text should not say "potjerali" but it should say "potisli." But if there is another word you want to introduce as well, I note you were cut off because of the time the other day, and I give you that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing to come up with and use different words. What I have here in three documents are three different words, and I stand by the wording that I provided. In some parts we extended the territory, and "potisli," "pushed back" the Muslims from the territory where they were practically the majority. The word that I used at that time could only be "potisli," "pushed back." Another thing that I would like to emphasise is the following: You see, I'm not saying where they are a majority. I'm saying where they are practically a majority. I have here in front of me that speech as well, and I also have the statistics. At the moment when I was speaking, that is to say, at the 17th Assembly session, we did not have under our control a single local commune out of the 20 Ilidza local communes where the Muslims were a majority. In 11 local communes -- in the 11 local communes that we held there was a Christian majority. In some of them there's not a single Muslim. Muslims hold five local communes with an enormous population. The Croats hold two local communes with a population that is somewhat smaller than ours, and they have their own municipality there. In the territories that we have under our control in 11 local communes, at that time there was 5.858 Muslims according to the census from 1991. And in the areas that were held by the Muslims, according to the 1991 census, there were 6.943 Serbs. That is to say, over 1.000 Serbs more, whereas in the Croat-held territory there was 1.724 Serbs. That is to say, over 2.000 Serbs remained in territories that were under the control of the Croats and Muslims. As for Croats, I am not going to speak about them. We were not at war with them, and it doesn't really matter, but in August and September, the Muslims seized two -- two local communes from them, Stup and Otes, and practically they pushed them back in military terms, and then civilians fell victim and there was fierce fighting between the Serbs and Muslims on the borders between these local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, by the time of the 17th Assembly session in July of 1992, was -- did you know that division from the Muslims was or was not a goal of Republika Srpska and the Republika Srpska leadership?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our primary goal in an Ilidza was defence and self-defence of our own ethnic areas. It is quite clear when it was established that it was impossible to live in a dignified and peaceful manner with mutual respect. Then everybody protected their own territory, and in a way, what was opted for was division.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was division an express goal of the Republika Srpska authorities?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that ultimately, and I cannot give a specific answer to that, because everything I would say would be maybe yes in some periods or in some previous periods no. Certainly in the pre-war period, no, but as the war went on, it became obvious that in the Muslim part there were quite a few fundamentalists, extremists with whom it was not easy to live, even for the autochthonous Muslims, let alone Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ever hear of the strategic goals, Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you knew about the strategic goals by the time you gave this speech in July of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when I exactly knew, but possibly it was in a Official Gazette that we received these strategic goals. Perhaps there was mention of it beforehand too. It was well known when the Official Gazette was published, and if it was published in the Official Gazette, then that would be that moment. I mean the mail would arrive in three or four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me see if I can perhaps refresh your recollection about when you might have heard about the strategic goals. Do you recall, for example, that the strategic goals were made known through the participants of the Assembly and even through others, for example, through the people's deputy?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I mean the strategic goals, when they were adopted by the Assembly, they were published in the Official Gazette. As soon as we received the Official Gazette, we read that. The deputy who was there, if he was there, if he participated in that Assembly when they were adopted, could have told us about it too. However, the Ilidza leadership and the Ilidza people did not meddle in high-level politics. We were always prepared, before the war and during the war, and that was shown by Dayton as well, that we are prepared to accept what high-level politics agrees upon, and what was agreed upon in Dayton was fatal for Ilidza, and about 20.000 Serbs were moved out on the eve of the application of the Dayton agreement, that is to say from the western part --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, excuse me, but if we don't want to be here for the next month, please try to answer my questions rather than elaborate by moving from 1992 into 1996. I don't want to prevent you from answering questions, but I am asking you not to expound on subjects that haven't been raised. Now, during the course of your previous interviews, you had an opportunity to see an Official Gazette in which the strategic objectives were promulgated and to see that that was in 26 -- that was in November of 1993, more than a year after the discussion of the strategic objectives at the 16th Assembly in May of 1992. You recall seeing that Official Gazette and having it presented to you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but you see, I don't remember the date. However, when I skipped all the way to 1996, I was trying to say that we did not meddle in high-level politics but that we accepted it unconditionally, whatever was agreed upon, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And going back to the discussion and the question I just raised, when you were shown that Official Gazette and when saw it and saw that it was in November of 1993, did you then clarify that the decision was known through the participants of the Assembly and was known to us through the people's deputy and through political meetings, because there were many meetings of the leadership of the Serb people from Pale with people from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, it's very hard for me to explain all of that. However, the procedure in the Assembly is practically this: The professional staff prepares material, then a meeting of the deputies' club is held, and then all of this goes before the Assembly. It's not a long period of time within the Assembly from these initial meetings until the actual session of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with respect to Assembly sessions that you did not attend, you'd get information back from those who did, including the deputy or a Member of Parliament; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, information arrived through the Official Gazette. Secondly, from our Member of Parliament, Ljubo Bosiljcic, if he was present and to the extent to which he thought it was necessary to provide information. There were no other ways. Perhaps if somebody attended as a guest, as I attended the 17th session, and the other presidents of the Sarajevo municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the strategic goals call for the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean I cannot remember that now. If we talked about the strategic objectives in Mr. Krajisnik's case, I mean, for me not to say something in a different way, then I accept what I said there and then, because I remembered better then. Now I could not say just off-the-cuff what any one of the strategic objectives was except that perhaps there is some mention of the Neretva River, and I was born on the banks of the Neretva and lived on the banks of the Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware that the division of Sarajevo was part of the strategic goals or part of the objective of Republika Srpska and the Republika Srpska authorities, when you were speaking in July of 1992, for example?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't thinking about the strategic objectives then. You said that they were published in 1993. That is to say, I didn't even know about them. However, every Serb who was in Sarajevo in the ethnic areas where Serbs had lived for centuries wanted to have these areas remain Serb and asked the leadership to reach agreement with the Muslim leadership in order to have these areas remain Serb. People kept asking me too: "Has Ilidza been sold out? Will Ilidza stay in Serb hands or will it be handed over to the Muslims by way of some agreement," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We talked the other day about agreement by hook or crook, that is -- not agreement, about division by hook or crook. That was at transcript page 12994. That is, either division by agreement or division by force of arms to free or liberate territories which Serbs believed belonged to them. Did anyone at the 17th Assembly session, Mr. Prstojevic, speak about division of Sarajevo either by agreement or, if not, by force of arms?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I did not attend that session until the very end, and I did not really pay much attention to what other MPs were saying. When I finished my speech, I left, either immediately or after some time, because the Assembly session went on for a long time. I think it went on for several days. However, in this speech of mine, which I have here, I said, among other things, that the Serb municipalities in the western area are surrounded by a double encirclement and that food cannot arrive. At the end of the speech, and that's what you're interested in, I said, and I'm reading this verbatim.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We don't have the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you look further on: "I kindly ask high-level politics to tell us very nicely whether the peace process can bring a division to Sarajevo in an appropriate way so that we know. If not, let us take up arms to free the territories that we consider to be our own. Otherwise -- or, rather, because otherwise, there may be an unprecedented genocide against the Serb people in Sarajevo in that area." That's the end of the quote. Let me just say this: Where we did not defend our ethnic areas by military means, there was practically a genocide, like in Pofalici, where everyone was killed and only one Muslim soldier lost his life. Over 300 civilians were killed there. That is what I said, not having in mind any strategic objectives or anything. That is to say, my personal view and my personal position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what did you understand was meant by "division," Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to explain here what I meant, what my understanding was and what the Serbs in that area thought. Where there is an ethnic Serb majority according to the census, the 1991 census, our wish was for that to be our Serb Sarajevo, that we be in a decision-making position there and that there is no out-voting of anyone by anyone. After all, Dayton divided Sarajevo into the eastern and western parts. Five Ilidza local communes will, in fact, remain in the eastern part -- or, rather, Serb Sarajevo. Some municipalities in their entirety, like Pale. Others, Trnovo, Stari Grad, Centar, in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware of demographic concerns about the Muslim birth rate and the number of -- and the proliferation or the propagation or the increase in the Muslim population in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and particularly in portions of Bosnia and Herzegovina that the Serbs considered to be their ethnic territory?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Ilidza we have information from the 1991 census. We have the number of inhabitants, the ethnic composition, the number of households, the number of livestock, everything. I'm not an expert. I never thought about the birth rate, and I really do not know anything about that. Even more so because my parents had ten children, and I am their seventh child.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware that others did think about the birth rate, including members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, and made their concerns about the birth rate of the Muslims known to the other members of the SDS and of Republika Srpska authorities?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, please. I cannot guess. I cannot answer such questions. But I do know that, to this day, the Muslims have a low birth rate and that they go hand-in-hand with the Serbs as far as that's concerned, that we are on a totally equal footing there, equals. Mr. Tieger, this is the first time I come across a question like that. Please. I cannot think about that. I couldn't think about it at the time either. Time did not allow me to do that, nor was there any need to think about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand that's the position you want to take, Mr. Prstojevic. I wasn't asking you at all to guess. Let's go back now to the transcript of the 17th Assembly session, which you attended. You told us earlier that Mr. Ostojic was the president of the SDS Executive Board and a resident of Ilidza who was "at our disposal without limitations." He spoke at that Assembly session. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, it is true that Mr. Ostojic was a resident of Ilidza and that it was possible to contact him at all times. However, I don't know what he spoke about at the Assembly session. I know that Mr. Ostojic is married to a Muslim woman, and I know that his wife and their two sons spent the whole war with us in Ilidza, in the central neighbourhood of Ilidza known as Vito.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me give you -- those are interesting details about Mr. Ostojic, but not exactly focused on the question I asked. At the 17th Assembly session, and the transcript of that session is in evidence, Mr. Prstojevic, he was speaking about certain territory and the number of Serbs, the number of Muslims -- the percentage of Serbs, the percentage of Muslims, and the percentage of Croats. And then he said: "Through birth rate, within ten years you will lose even that percentage." That's at page 81 in the English of that session and page 83. Do you recall hearing Mr. Ostojic refer to the birth rate at that session?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. It seems that Mr. Tieger is now impeaching his witness, and I would ask that the Chamber decide whether that's permissible or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, first of all, that's not something that could be known, as the Court pointed out earlier, until the witness answers a question. The witness may say, "Thank you very much for reminding me about that. I had previously forgotten." It may turn out to be in the nature of additional information which contradicts a position the witness is taking, but we won't know that. Secondly, I will point out once again that I don't believe there's a system in the world that calls upon either party to make a question-by-question request to the Court to put questions to a witness. If there's a concern about whether or not questions that add to, clarify, illuminate or even contradict a witness's previous information, that's something that is indeed in the Court's hands, but the Court is alert to that issue now, has approved of the manner in which this has been proceeding, and I think is receiving information to which its entitled and indeed obligated to get. The -- having Mr. Robinson rise at every point, interrupt examination and other consequences, I think is not merely inefficient, but I think it undercuts the utility, purpose and ultimate value of an examination and the illumination the Court will receive from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tieger, I don't think Mr. Robinson is rising at every point.
