Generally speaking, of course, if during the course of an examination-in-chief there are questions which are asked in order to clarify or illuminate an answer, that's a perfectly standard technique. Where you get into the realm of contradiction, however, it is an impeachment or it may be an impeachment and I accept your point that until the witness gives an answer, you don't know whether it's necessary to go down that road or not. In order to be as efficient as possible, what I would say is that it seems to the Court at the moment that you are likely to be going down the road of impeachment, and there is a continuing authority from the Court to do so, but if you are going to do so in a very radical manner, by putting, for instance, a completely contradictory document, it would be useful, I think, for you to make that plain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I trust I try to be as both progressive and transparent in this process as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: We will have to understand that this is not a jury trial and we have to see and assess everything at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I quite agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, the question was whether you recall hearing Mr. Ostojic refer to the birth rate of Muslims or Croats at that 17th Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that you said that Mr. Ostojic and his speech were recorded on page 81 of the minutes of the meeting of the Assembly session. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's in the English, Mr. Prstojevic. That's 83 in the B/C/S. But I'm not asking you to read it out. I'm asking you first if you recall it.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it, because my speech was recorded on page 68 of B/C/S version. Mr. Tieger, I would like to remind you now that in 2003 as well, I told your investigators that upon finishing my speech, due to some prior commitments I had to leave. However, you are pursuing the same practice that you pursued in the Krajisnik case by saying that I said something, for example, during interview in this way and then later I changed it, and after giving it some thought over the past two days and on the basis of the documents that I have with me, I decided that this is not the case. I understand this to be a psychological pressure exerted on me to disrupt my concentration, to stop me from thinking and providing proper answers to the best of my knowledge and recollection. In other words, I'd like to say that I didn't hear Mr. Ostojic talking about this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we're all under constraints of time. If you can attempt simply to answer the question that is asked, whether it's coming from Mr. Tieger or, in due course, from Dr. Karadzic, we would all get along much more efficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You do recall, Mr. Prstojevic, that you had an opportunity to look at video coverage of a meeting or convention in 1991 at which Mr. Ostojic spoke; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw it the other day during proofing here in The Hague. On the last day of proofing, in fact. I saw a meeting of the local board -- or, rather, the Assembly of the Dobrinja SDS local board where Mr. Ostojic spoke and delivered a speech as a guest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could call up 40132, and I'd like to listen to a portion that I believe -- well, first of all, show the very beginning of it so that we can see Mr. Ostojic. And you identified this speaker as Mr. Ostojic; is that right? At the point at which he greets everyone on behalf of the SDS Main Board and Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the speaker here on this device, in this image. However, on the 2nd of March of this year I saw this footage for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And viewing the portion of the footage that you had an opportunity to see at that time, you did indicate that the speaker was Mr. Ostojic. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could play a portion of the video at 20:11.4 through 20:21.2, and I think for the benefit of the interpreters, that should be found on page 8 in approximately the middle of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot find the exact portion in the transcript. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Could you pause that, please, for a moment. Well, it would -- if I can assist the interpreters. At approximately the -- I mean, we can go back and do it quickly. At approximately the -- just above the middle of the page you should in capital letters the name Izetbegovic and immediately below that "51 per cent."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we have found it. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can commence again. It might be the easiest thing to do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We can prevent what's in Izetbegovic's declaration. And it says that this will be an Islamic state when there's 51 per cent of them. That's being cooked, for us, gentlemen. That's what we are being told."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have lost the sound. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The text appears to be coming up in English in any event.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "That's what we were being told. We /unintelligible/ are not in a hurry /unintelligible/ my grandchild does not have to live to be in an Islamic state, but he will /unintelligible/ with the intention to Islamic Bosnia to /unintelligible/ and we, gentlemen, are in a state of prenatal genocide. One Serb family, two heads and one child. Well, there's two of them, but at neighbour Sejo ... seven. Therefore, another thing: We hope that this fixation, this absurd political idea of the Serb people called Yugoslavism will disappear. And --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we can stop the tape there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, the reference to "a state of prenatal genocide. One Serb family, one child. But at neighbour Sejo's ... seven," is that a reference to the concern over the Muslim birth rate?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't hear at all what Mr. Ostojic was saying, probably due to some technical reasons. I don't know why. Secondly, I heard this speech on the 2nd of March, and I understood that my task was solely to confirm the identity of the speaker, and I didn't bother too much to listen what he was saying, and I didn't make any note of it. Thirdly, as a farmer and a pensioner, I don't have any capacity or competence to comment on a speech delivered by, I think, Professor Ostojic, delivered in 1991. That would be inappropriate and impolite. That is not true. For example, I have three children. My younger brother has four children. And it was not exactly true that each Serbian family had one child only.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Last question on that subject, Mr. Prstojevic. Are you -- is it your position that you never heard any expression of concern about demographics and the unfavourable demographics from the Serbian point of view, including the Muslim birth rate, from any member of the SDS or Republika Srpska leadership?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kindly ask you not to try and make me remember that. I cannot remember that at the moment. But by watching television, and I watch TV Belgrade most of the time, I hear that there is a lot of talk about birth rate in Serbia, but I cannot remember that there was any such discussion about birth rates and things of that sort before the war or during the war for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The discussion at the 17th Assembly session was about the meeting in Ilidza at April 18th. When did you next see Mr. Karadzic after that meeting? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot recall exactly, but there were certain meetings, mainly in the latter part of 1992, where President Karadzic was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not talking about the latter part of 1992, but let's see if -- since you can't recall exactly, let me see if it assists you to hear what you said in 2005. There was a discussion of that meeting in April. You made reference to subsequent meetings in Pale, and then you were asked: "How long after this meeting in Ilidza did you then go to Pale?" You said: "I cannot remember really." This is page 28 of the English. And page 47 of 65 ter 22231. "I cannot remember really, but I think it was in May, but what is important is that Vojo Djordjevic was still the commander of -- he was still the commander of Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and he was in Lukavica at that time when went to Pale. That was around the 10th of May roughly." Then you were asked what's the importance of him and you said that's part of the chronology of events or helps you fix the date. Then you were asked how often -- just a rough guide, how often were you invited to Pale, and you said invitations to go to Pale were more and more often as the war was progressing. More or less immediately from the 10th of May, there was another meeting held in Pale. And can you confirm, Mr. Prstojevic, that that's what you said, or does that refresh your recollection about a meeting at or around the 10th of May in 1992 in Pale with Mr. Karadzic and others?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my documents I have the date of that meeting, and I remember it because for a short while I saw the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, but his name was Vojislav Djurdjevac, not Vojo Djordjevic. And during the break I think I can locate this date in my papers. I know that all presidents of city municipalities were in attendance at that meeting and that the presidents of the city municipalities were extremely dissatisfied with the leadership because the seat of the government had remained in Pale. And I can find in my notes exactly that we criticised the leadership and they criticised us back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned that -- in that interview that invitations to go to Pale were more and more often as the war progressed. What was discussed at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is absolutely true. As war progressed, the meetings became more and more frequent. The purpose of the majority of meetings, or maybe all of them, except the first one, where there was rifts, as I said, in the majority of meetings the military situation was discussed and also the political situation, but it only had to do with high politics. So what was discussed was military and political situation. Secondly, there were requests made by the leadership to us, what we needed in terms of logistics, what was needed by the military and what the ordinary people needed. There were also discussions about co-operation at the local level between the civilian authorities, the army, and the MUP and how to bring the rule of law about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition to personal contact by, for example, going to Pale, did you also have communication with the leadership through other means such as the telephone?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember my personal contacts mainly. At the time when telephone service was active and functioning, of course we communicated over the telephone whenever it was necessary and if we could reach the relevant people that we wanted to speak to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And telephone service was active and functioning in, for example, April and May 1992; is that right? And you've had a chance to see large numbers of telephone conversations in which you participated during that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I state an objection? I think this is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, there's an answer to the question. I can re-ask it. If -- in light of the number of intercepts already tendered and reviewed, if that's at issue, I'll be -- I can re-ask the question, although I think we have an answer to it. We have a proofing note in which the witness confirmed his participation in, I think, dozens, or at least over 20, conversations. We've seen it in the transcript, but I'm in your hands, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I was simply seeking your observation. It strikes me that it -- the question doesn't actually fall into the classic example of a leading question. It gives an alternative and then makes an inquiry, but if you can rephrase it, so much the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask this in light of the fact that the question has been answered, let me ask: Can you give us an example of some of the people you were in contact with, for example, that is what organisations or bodies they were associated with, and I have in mind, for example, JNA officials, MUP officials, RS political authorities in Pale, other municipal leaders around Sarajevo and so on? Can you give us an example of some of the people you were in contact with, either referring to the specific conversations you listened to the other day or others that you may have in mind?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the local level of our municipality there were continuous telephone contacts with brigade commanders, with the people from the JNA, up until the 19th of May, and then from the 19th of May with the corps command, with people from our -- some 20 local communes, and so on. But when the phones were working and there was contact with the government in Pale and our leadership in Pale, if there was any need, we didn't hesitate to call the leadership in Pale, meaning the members of government, certain ministers, and other state functionaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you have contact with other local leaders around Sarajevo in other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I had asked you about the Crisis Staffs the other day. After the -- during the course -- well, let me ask you this question: Did -- were the Crisis Staffs replaced by another body, and did that body -- well, first of all, was the Crisis Staff replaced by another body?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The War Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did the War Commissioner have -- did the War Commissioner -- or who was the War Commissioner in -- in Ilidza, and did that person have any connection to the Republika Srpska leadership?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first War Commissioner for the Serbian municipality of Ilidza and for the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac was Miroslav Radovanovic, who had a master's degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came to us, to Ilidza, meaning that he was sent by the leadership in Pale. I don't know which organ formed the War Commissioner's office. He introduced himself, and he began to help us in our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall the War Commissioner for Vogosca and/or Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was Dr. Nikola Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you aware that the War Commissioner, Mr. Radovanovic, had been sent by the leadership in Pale?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And how would you characterise, then, the level of control that the leadership in Pale had over the -- over Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a very difficult time. There was confusion, and we simply didn't know each other. Amongst ourselves in the Municipal Board, out of 38 people I only knew one before the Municipal Board was established. So then in the horizontal co-operation there were a lot sparks flying around the TO staff, the MUP, the civilian part, and the commissioner came practically to take a snapshot of the situation and to horizontally link up and co-ordinate. It meant that he could criticise somebody, and also he could harmonise the co-operation. Secondly, I understood that it was his goal to help us, to link up the co-operation, to aid, because Ilidza was complex. Ilidza only had two public security stations at two ends and a third police station somewhere in the middle. It had border police as well. So it had four police units. So simply, the need was to link all of that up and to have the rule of law start functioning again. Then he, as a person whose jurisdiction included us, had to also provide evaluations and assessments of us. Where were the problems? Who was responsible if -- if the co-operation was not good? Who was responsible if something was not working well? So that practically he was -- I could put it that way, first among equals, but he was above us because he could evaluate our work, but we couldn't evaluate his.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about something you said in 2005, at page 28 of the English, and page 47 of the B/C/S. Again, you were talking about meetings with Pale, and then you said: "Well, what's even more important is that they sent us war commissioners." And then you pointed out that Radovanovic was sent to Ilidza, Poplasen to Vogosca and Ilijas, and then you said: "So practically the leadership from Pale controlled the local municipality president or local leaderships through those war commissioners. They were sent there to be superior to the municipal organs." What was -- was that accurate, Mr. Prstojevic, and does that expand on the impact of the role of the commissioners?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the same thing but in a different way. It's quite clear that he is evaluating somebody -- or the person who he is evaluating somebody's work and submitting a report, they are positioned above the local leadership. The statements do match.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we had talked about meetings. Do you recall a meeting at Jahorina in September of 1992 or at some point in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you remember who attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The top state and political leadership was there, headed by President Karadzic, President Krajisnik, some ministers. I know that there was some Finance Minister, someone called Petra. I don't remember ministers, the other ones. Of the military leadership General Mladic was there, the commander of all Sarajevo brigades and headed by the corps commander, all municipal presidents, presidents of the Executive Boards. It was quite a big gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Prstojevic, I want to next ask you some questions following up on the comment that you read out from the 17th Assembly, asking what the division of Sarajevo would be and whether arms should be taken up to free the territories, which -- I think the quote was, "We believe are ours." So if I could turn first to a document I'd like to show you. But actually, before I do, I just wanted to ask you about something you said about the demographic situation in Ilidza. Where were the Muslim areas? And perhaps that's not a question that's a particular problem. Let me ask you first of all, were Butmir, Hrasnica, Sokolovic Kolonija, for example, Muslim-majority areas?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our decisions on the formation of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza of the 5th of April left out all the Muslim communities where the Muslims were in a majority, including Hrasnica 1, Hrasnica 2, Sokolovic Kolonija, Butmir, Stupsko Brdo, and a part of Kotorac, Donji Kotorac, where the Muslims are the majority population. We also left out Stup 1 as a whole and Otes. Let me correct myself. Stup 1, actually there is a part called Doglodi where the Serbs are a majority. That part was not included. But Stup 1 and Otes was given to the Croats and that's where they formed their municipality and the HVO until the Muslims drove them out, which is what I talked about earlier. The other local communes had a major Christian majority. I have a description here, and I can read it out precisely. There are some local communes where there is no -- not a single Muslim. There are some communities where there isn't a single Croat.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, the interpreters have asked that you repeat your last sentence. They couldn't either hear it or understand it.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. They didn't understand. It's a Serbian proverb. When people get on well together, we say like nail and flesh or cuticle. We managed somehow to stay without quarreling, but what high politics decides high politics does. But there was a lot of pressure on the Croats also, from the leadership from Zagreb and leadership from Bosnia, to enter into war against us, but they knew that this was not in their interest. They knew that we were not touching on their territories and they didn't want to do that, and I commend them for it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please just make it clear in this answer that the witness is talking about relationship between the Croats and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. We are talking about the relations between the Croats and the Serbs in Ilidza and the Croats from the municipality of Kiseljak where they are in a majority and they border on us. Some 11 kilometres of the border is an area that was never taken up by anyone, and we never had any incidents or excesses with them. We had local communities in Ilidza during the war where there were more Croats during the war than during peacetime. For example, the local community of Blazuj, where there were a lot of holiday homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we call up P01006.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I indicated I was going to show you a few documents from that time. While we're waiting for the English to be called up, I'll indicate to you, Mr. Prstojevic, that that is a document from the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Well, since I'm going through a series of documents, Your Honour, I don't know if we want to take an early break or not, but -- I'm getting a nod of assent from the Registrar, who thinks that might be a good idea in view of the technological difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think that's probably a very good idea. So we'll break now and sit again at 5 to the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I had previously called up P0111 -- P01006. I see it was already on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Prstojevic, I believe you've already been looking at that for the last few minutes, is that right? The September 12, 1992, Sarajevo-Romanija Corps document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: We don't have it on the monitor. Now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, just to commence again, that's a document dated 12 September 1992, from the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to the command of the SRK rear command post. And the preamble begins: "In the VRS Main Staff telegram dated September 7th, 1992, we received tasks from the conference on military and political matters in the SRK area held on 6 September 1992 on Jahorina ..." And then it goes on to describe the attendees, including the SRK command, brigade commanders, presidents of Municipal Assemblies, chiefs of municipal recruiting offices, members of the Main Staff, and members of the government and Presidency of the Serbian Republic. First, Mr. Prstojevic, is that a reference to the Jahorina meeting that you mentioned earlier when you described a meeting attended by, I believe you said, all municipal presidents, presidents of Executive Boards and so on?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, this was the first meeting of its kind at such a high level after the beginning of the war. A while ago, however, I commented and spoke about the different meeting of the same sort that was held sometime after this one. I don't remember exactly when. Concerning this document that I see in front of me, I would need to see the end of this document to see who signed it, and with an apology, I would like to remind you of a mistake made by Mr. Tieger, intentionally or unintentionally, when he said that at the Assembly session I asked how to divide Sarajevo. This is not true, and one can see from the minutes that I never asked anyone how to divide Sarajevo. Instead, I laid stress on a peaceful agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We have your words here in court, Mr. Prstojevic. We have your words on paper, and I'm sure the Court will be attendant to all of the information available to it. Now, this document was signed by Mr. Galic, commander of the SRK. And if it will assist you in -- I'm happy to look at the back of the document. And now I want to turn to the tasks that emerged from the meeting on Jahorina on the 6th of September, 1992, as reflected in this document, and, in particular, in paragraph 1 on the first page. It begins: "Ensure stubborn and decisive defence of the lines reached, improve the operational position," and so on. Then it concludes, turning to the portion beginning on the third line from the bottom: "... and liberate and take control of important parts of the city, features close to it (Mojmilo, Stup junction) and estates (Donji Kotorac, Hrasnica, Butmir, and Sokolovic Kolonija)." Now, first of all, those are the -- Hrasnica, Butmir, and Sokolovic Kolonija you identified as Muslim areas within Ilidza. Was Donji Kotorac also a Muslim area?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was, and it still is, under the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what about Gornji Kotorac? Had that been a Muslim area too?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kotorac is a single local commune in its own right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, there's a reference to Donji Kotorac. Was there a Gornji Kotorac as well?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one and the same neighbourhood. Kotorac was a local commune that had 1.950 inhabitants; 1.083 of them were Muslims and the rest was the Christian majority. The Muslims were mainly concentrated in Donji Kotorac, and in an enclave in Gornji Kotorac as well, which is within the Serbian-populated area. There are about 70 households there. So if you multiply that by 4, that makes up to 300 residents. However, this line, Butmir, Kotorac and Donji Kotorac and Ilaca, elevation 655 Crveni Klanac, et cetera, was strategically significant both for the Muslims and for us. And for that reason Gornji Kotorac and Srednji Kotorac were to become the area of permanent activity by artillery, and practically, the Muslim and the Serbian populations would be evacuated from that area. In Srednji and Gornji, a total of 41 civilians were killed, 39 Serbs and 2 Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn to another document quickly in connection with liberating certain areas of Ilidza, and that would be 65 ter 10773. Mr. Prstojevic, this is an excerpt from the minutes of the second Assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza, which was held on the 29th of August, 1992, as it indicates in the beginning of the document. It indicates that 41 deputies attended the session and you, president of the Assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza, opened the session. The agenda included an opening speech by the president of the Serbian municipality on the political and security situation, and in item 1 that opening speech is reflected, including information about, as we see on the fifth line from the -- below the heading "Item 1": "Military Command - realisation of wartime goals, defence and liberation of yet not-liberated territories." Do you recall that meeting, Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the second session of the Municipal Assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And does item 1 reflect you speaking to the persons assembled?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What were the wartime goals, and what were the yet not-liberated territories to which you referred?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our primary wartime goal was to defend the Serbian ethnic territories, and that wasn't an easy task at all. However, that is in line 4 where I make this specific reference. One has to look into the future with a certain degree of optimism. Given that the Muslim forces were attacking us constantly, we issued verbal threats, saying that we would also launch offensive operations against certain territories, but we never did that. And now I say that according to the order of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, I can say that units of Sarajevo-Romanija Corps never attacked Hrasnica 1, Hrasnica 2, Sokolovic Kolonija or Butmir with a view to taking possession of these territories. Furthermore, pursuant to our decision to establish the Serbian municipality, these local communes that I named, including Stupsko Brdo and Donji Kotorac, were not part of our municipality. However, in parliamentary debates, if any of the deputies was satisfied by what somebody said but we thought that was irrelevant and not worthy of implementation, that could become a conclusion. The person who proposed it would write a conclusion but it would just remain on paper. I was surprised to see that this is what the Main Staff said, because we would not do it, but I know, and in the conclusions from this particular Assembly session, one can find approximately identical things, but there is no evidence that we every launched any offensives against these territories. We stand by it, and you can ask the Muslims to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, just a brief technical problem. Just turning quickly to page 2. There's reference there in the item marked number 1, and I think that's what you're referring to in talking about various conclusions, to the "Proposal of decisions from the meeting of the Deputies' Club: "1. In order to free and complete the territory of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza it is necessary to urgently coordinate operations for establishing of the corridor - route through Lukavica." And for that important task, co-ordination between all military units, the public security station, et cetera, would be necessary. Through what territory did that corridor discussed here through to Lukavica go?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to read a sentence that you intentionally left out from the second paragraph, which reads: "In order to complete this important task, it is necessary to establish co-ordination between all military authorities, and to ensure," that you left out, "unity of command over all armed forces, armed groups and individuals." I would like to underline that this demonstrates that we did not support any paramilitary units. Now, back to your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prstojevic. Before you go on, I'd like to say one thing to you. I think I've treated you with a great deal of courtesy. This document is in front of the Court. I specifically referred to that sentence, and I would ask you to refrain from allegations and accusations, especially when they're so unfounded. And I will try to maintain an appropriate decorum here and I urge you to do the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I endorse that which Mr. Tieger has said. The role of witness is to answer questions honestly and impartially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, I endorse what Mr. Tieger and my colleague has said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then I apologise to Mr. Tieger. Why do we have this conclusion? In this month, and I'll check the exact date, the Serbian leadership handed over Butmir airport in Sarajevo that had been under our control of our forces, and this is where the traffic ran along the tarmac between the eastern and western parts of Ilidza. However, after the airport was handed over to the UN international forces, for quite some time, I don't know whether it was a year or more, we were not able to travel along that route, but, rather, we had to go around the entire Sarajevo in westerly and north-westerly direction as well as a north-easterly direction in order to reach that particular point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, excuse me. Sorry to interrupt, but you're clearly reading from a document. What is that document?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document -- what you have on the screen I am holding in my hand a hard copy of that, and I'm reading from it. So this is an excerpt from the minutes of meeting of the second Assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza. I'm just reading. I'm not inventing this. I've just moved on a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's not a problem. If you could just let us know when you're -- when you're doing so. It's so everyone knows what's happening at any given time. I'm not trying to preclude you from referring to documents you've brought. If you're looking at a particular document, if you can just let us know what it is.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's this document. Now, I can tell you that in my briefcase I have all my testimonies from 2003, 2005, and 2006, as well as my testimony in the Krajisnik case and the proofing notes. That's why I have so many documents in this briefcase. Secondly, when I came here, I started writing something about the winter period in Ilidza, and I have these notes here with me, and I can consult them whenever it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can be of assistance. I -- I suppose the witness said, "I'm not reading. I'm just telling you. I'm just looking at the conclusions."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The essence was that the deputies asked for a corridor to be opened towards Lukavica, instead of travelling for three hours and being exposed to fire from Lukavica. Let us look at the tasks assigned to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and its brigade, and it will not be done. This corridor would not be open until the end of the war, because in the meantime, UNPROFOR allowed us certain slots for crossing across the tarmac. And this could only refer to the fighting in Dobrinja, not Butmir, because Butmir is a neighbourhood where indigenous people live and these people were nice and they attacked us and they -- otherwise they wouldn't have attacked us had that not been ordered by the leadership.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again I have to ask for a clarification. The witness said that "we were being shot at on our way to Lukavica," and in the transcript it says that fire was going Lukavica -- no, opened towards Lukavica. Did the witness -- to fire from Lukavica. No. Fire from Lukavica could not have targeted the Serbian corridor. Can we clarify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point is that that was a route that took three hours to cover between Rajlovac, Vogosca, Pale, and finally Lukavica. Certain areas were covered by snipers and by machine-gun fire, and everybody who was travel along that route risked their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to show you another document, Mr. Prstojevic, but before I do let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am not complaining particularly about this intervention, but I think it's -- it should be noted that the proper way of making an intervention of that sort is to note simply the problem area and ask for clarification rather than providing what the accused thinks the answer should or must be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: In principle that must be right, Mr. Tieger, but on the other hand, if there has been an error, the earlier it's pointed out the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, as I say, Your Honour, I've no problems with interventions to seek needed clarifications to the transcript, but I think it's important that we don't get in the habit of doing it in a way that could cause problems. Can we turn, please, to 65 ter 09 -- 0898 -- oh, and I tender this document, Mr. President. The previous document, 10773. And I would also tender the portion of the video-clip from before, which was 04132.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning video-clip, I think that the witness only identified the speaker. He couldn't contribute anything about the views and positions of Mr. Ostojic, and I'm also making this point as a matter of principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: He nevertheless did identify the speaker, and for that purpose at least the video should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The video will be Exhibit P2448, and the document 10773 will be Exhibit P2449.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I wanted to turn next to 65 ter 0989. And perhaps before we get into that document -- into -- I think this might be the wrong one in any event. Let me ask you a question about the corridor you referred to. Do you recall when that corridor was to be opened and when there were initial -- and when there were initial attempts to do so?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one attempt, and that happened when the Muslims mounted an offensive in June 1992 against us, and it started precisely on the 8th of June, 1992, by an attack launched on all ethnic neighbourhoods around Sarajevo. At the same time, an offensive was launched from the outside as well. The municipality of Nova Sarajevo-Lukavica came under fierce attack, also part of Lukavica defended by the Ilidza forces, Kasindol from inside and from outside, Vojkovici, Grlica, Krupac, and Kotorac. The middle part of the latter village. In the fighting that took place on that day, the 1st Corps sustained the highest losses according to the information provided in the book --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name of the author of the book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After our forces stabilised, which took about five or six days of fighting --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, not yet and I may not at all ask you for the details of the corridor operation. Let's take it a step at a time, okay? Did the proposals for opening the corridor include the prospects of an attack on Butmir or Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Butmir? Never. But Dobrinja. I was just about to say that when we repelled the attacks that went on for about 30 days, the fighting went on for 30 days, then our army launched an offensive in the Aerodromsko Naselje part of Dobrinja, and Dobrinja 1 and Dobrinja 4. And that is when an attempt was made to open the corridor in that area. Fighting went on for a few days. The Muslim forces were pushed away in one area. About 2.000 to 2.100 housing units were taken, and one stayed there throughout the war in defence. So an attempt was made to break through the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You said Butmir never. Did you never hear about, were you never consulted about the idea to attack Butmir?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, it was never our understanding that we were waging war against all Muslims. Rather, against Muslim fanatics and fundamentalists. Butmir is a neighbourhood where people have lived for a long, long time, and if someone wanted to take Butmir, it would have been easy prey for the Serbian Army. However, we were against that. Every neighbour, every inhabitant of Butmir was against that. That is to say, the entire leadership, and we never attacked Butmir militarily. Also, when the first part of 1992 was over, they didn't attack us either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's try 65 ter 09 -- 08989 once again. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, this is a document I believe you've seen before. It's headed "Republika Srpska SDS, Ilidza SDS Municipal Board." Entitled "The declaration of the agenda of Ilidza SDS for working in wartime." Arising from a meeting held on the 6th of February, 1993, at which the Municipal Board of Ilidza SDS adopted its agenda for working in wartime. And you are familiar with this document; is that correct, Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm holding that document in my hands. It's a document of local nature. It is from the Municipal Board of the SDS of Ilidza, and it is it is quite literally the programme declaration of the SDS Ilidza for working in wartime conditions. As for this document, we adopted it as our own initiative and no one asked us to adopt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the document?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, absolutely. This is it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have great trouble hearing the witness. Could all microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is the declaration in any respect inconsistent with your understanding of the position of the RS authorities or the SDS Main Board at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're not -- or, rather, I am the main author of this text. When writing this, I did not have the positions of the Main Board of the SDS at all. I just had a small working team, and all of us together had worked out an outline, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand that, but you stressed that it was a local document, and I was simply asking you if in any respects you considered this document that you were primarily responsible for to be inconsistent with or incompatible with the positions of the RS republic authorities or the SDS republic authorities.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I haven't really given this any thought, but I think that it is not inconsistent but barely -- basically, what I was bearing in mind was the local interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 again refers to liberated and strengthened control over all Serb ethnic territories. It also, in the last sentence of paragraph 3, refers to the significant help that the Serb people of Ilidza led by the SDS gave to Serbs on the territories of other municipalities of Srpsko Sarajevo. What were you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, please. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: What is your objection, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The learned Mr. Tieger said that this has to do with liberation. However, this actually has to do with defence, and that may affect the witness. The Serb people of the -- the Serb people of Ilidza led by the SDS defended --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- did not liberate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt in that fashion, Your Honour, but I raised in principle the objection to commentary and giving evidence in the guise of an objection. I think that's precisely what's happening here, and objections should not be framed in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Tieger beat me to it. This is just again a question of commenting by you and an attempt to give evidence. Comments such as this have no evidential value, and the basis of your objection is one which I think is minimal and one which the Court cannot sustain.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just explain why? May I just say what my understanding was? My understanding was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you asked if you may, and the answer is at the moment that you may not. Please allow Mr. Tieger to continue. If there are matters which you want to put into cross-examination in due course on this topic, you are, of course, free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, again, what were you referring to when you referred to the significant help that the Serb people of Ilidza led by the SDS gave to Serbs on the territories of other municipalities of Srpsko Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, that is quite clear. The Serb parts are an integral whole. When armed combat operations took place, we transferred Territorial Defence units from one part of the municipality and city to another through the agreement reached by Territorial Defence commanders or on the basis of agreements reached by commanders of Crisis Staffs. Had Ilidza not transferred forces from the eastern to the western part, we would have collapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page, please. The previous page contained the declaration. This page contains the tasks according to the agenda. And the first sentence below that states: "A black-winged vulture is looming over our Serb land on which we have lived from times immemorial. It is threatening to crush our Serb name, Serb culture, and Serb places of worship and to reduce Serbia to the Belgrade pashalic." And it continues -- well, first of all, let me ask you, what is that a reference to? Who is the black-winged vulture looming over Serb land?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, we Serbs speak in terms of symbols. This dragon threatens man with death. Several hundred years ago, the Serbian empire collapsed, and since then, poetry has said that all of Serbdom was doomed because of a seven-headed dragon. That is lethal danger in terms of the biological survival of our people in a certain area. This is still the introductory part, but it is truthful because many settlements were practically razed to the ground in Sarajevo, killing all the inhabitants. I've already mentioned Pofalici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you aware of any Bosnian Serb military operations in which Bosnian Muslim or Bosnian Croat civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably there were such operations, but at that point in time we were following the media very seldom because we didn't have time. War was being waged day and night. However, there were crimes probably on all three sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Return to the document. Now, the task of the Ilidza SDS also outlined where the legal authority of Ilidza Serb municipality is to be established, and that's in section 1.2. And that appears to contain -- to include what are referred to -- referred to as the non-liberated parts of Dobrinja, Vojnicko Polje, Serb Trnovo, Butmir, Hrasnica, Sokolovic Kolonija, and parts of Serb Kiseljak. That was among the tasks arising from the agenda of the Ilidza SDS?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what is written here, and this is what it says further on: "While achieving this objective, protect loyal non-Serb population to a maximum. Parts of Kiseljak, there are 700 Serbs living there." They were never a subject of dispute between us and the municipality of Kiseljak. To this day they have gone on living in the municipality of Kiseljak, and there was no war there. I've already said that we did not attack Butmir. We did not attack Hrasnica, Vojnicko Polje. We did not attack -- I've already spoken about Dobrinja, parts of Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would tender this --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, you're not finished?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't finished. Part of Trnovo -- parts of Trnovo will be Serb ethnic areas liberated in July 1993. However, we were not issuing orders. It is well known who starts military operations. This was our wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And now I tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2450, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I'd like to turn our attention next to some of the intercepts that you've both heard before and indeed commented on before, I believe, and including some of those that you asked an opportunity to comment on again. So let me first turn our attention to P1086. Now, I want you to take a look at that quickly. I'll walk you through it in a moment, but you may recognise it immediately because you've had a chance to both listen and -- listen to the audio and hear and read the transcript before, but it's a conversation that you have with first someone referred to as Mrki and then with a certain Novakovic. And as we see on the first page, toward the bottom, you indicate: "Why did Miki phone me?" Milenko says: "Phoned you to check with these people in Kotorac." Milenko says: "What should we do with them?" You ask: "Did you arrest them? What did you do?" And continuing on to the second page. There are continuing questions about whether those people had been arrested. Milenko says: "Down there on the road, all of them. Men are separated from the women." He says he's just received the word men are in the Kula prison and women went in the direction of Butmir. You tell him to put Tepavcevic on and he puts on Novakovic. He'll talk to you. You ask: "Have you been cleaning Kotorac today?" He says: "They have. I don't know the exact details because I was engaged otherwise." Then continuing the conversation, you say: "That's okay, but tell me, please, I beg of you, why did you take women to Butmir?" Novakovic says: "They said women were not in Butmir, but --" He says: "Well, in Butmir, yes, not to KP Dom but to Butmir. That's where they're going." And you say: "They cannot go to Butmir. We'll mop up," or cistite [phoen], "Butmir in time ..." And you continue, now on the third page: "Butmir will be mopped up. Sokolovic will be mopped up. Hrasnica will be mopped up." Again Novakovic says: "Well, I don't know where to take them." You say: "Well, there's Bascarsija. Please take them all to Bascarsija on foot." Novakovic says: "Aha." You say: "Women." Novakovic says: "Okay, now I'll --" And you say: "And men to prison." Novakovic says: "Okay, I'll check with him now and then I'll let you know." And then you say: "Yes. Tell them, those who convert to Orthodox religion on the spot, they can stay, women and children." Novakovic says: "Aha, okay, okay." And you say: "Do it, please, but don't make mistakes. You've done an excellent job, but it means that Butmir will be mopped up in time. Tell that to the people there." And then the conversation concludes as the two of you sign off. Mr. Prstojevic, you recall this conversation?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall this conversation. At first I had disputed it in 2003, and I needed an entire day. It was only on the following day, when I refreshed my memory, when I realised what had happened, I heard my voice. It was only then that I accepted that this was my conversation and that I could comment on it. So I accept that. But another thing, you have briefly recounted this conversation. According to the way you recounted it, I'm as black as a raven. If one elaborates on this speech analytically, one comes to something different. The real, actual state of affairs. That's what I did best in 2003. I have that in my briefcase here, because I had enough time. However, this is the gravest document that Ilidza has. In order to get the right picture, because there are omitted words and sentences in the text, there are also mistakes in the translation. I have here before me this conversation. I got it from you in 2005. I would like the original conversation to be heard before this Honourable Trial Chamber so that I could make corrections in terms of the omissions that were made and then analytically explain the -- the conversation. So here I am and here are the paragraphs of the law too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm -- okay. A couple things, Mr. Prstojevic. First of all, I read from the transcript. I didn't sort of recount it as you say. So can you identify right now some of the -- and you say what I read indicates that you're black as a raven. Do you want to read out now the good-guy portions of that intercept?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you that I sleep peacefully and that people from this neighbourhood visited me after the war as neighbours. But I would like the conversation to be heard, and it is only then that I can comment upon the conversation. As for the Trial Chamber, I will explain to them what symbols are, what reality is, and what is transcended, although you have read it out, because it's quite clear I say "women and children." The frail ones. All of those who are not military-age men can stay. But if it's just in the context of a sentence, then you sort of neglect it, and what you put in the focus is receiving the Orthodox faith. Starting from the Serb uprisings against the Turks, from the early 1800s, we are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, is this a line that the Prosecution wants to elaborate on at this particular juncture?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not particularly, Your Honour, but I don't -- I don't shrink from playing the intercept, and I -- it appears that the Prosecution is being challenged as omitting portions of the intercept or referring only to particular portions. I'm certainly in the Court's hands in that -- in that respect. As far as I'm concerned, it's a document that speaks quite sufficiently on its own. I'm happy that the witness is free to comment on it, but I don't know that we need to dwell on it for an undue period of time, but I am in the Court's hands in that way. As I say, I do not shrink in any way from playing this intercept in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Witness, you started off your answers in respect of this intercept by saying that you didn't remember it. It seems to me that you're now saying that you accept that it is your words, that you were a participant in the conversation which has been recorded, but you are now saying that the full content of what you said has not been incorporated into the transcript. Am I right in that analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, in 2003, I did not accept this conversation as mine on the first day because I only had the transcript, and it looked to me as if it was combined of three parts. However, in 2003, I did accept that as a conversation of mine with an unknown person, because he introduced himself under a code-name, and I still don't know who that is. However, we did not use code-names or pseudonyms during the war. Now, why I want to have this conversation played, to point out the places that were omitted by the interpreter and to clarify the conversation, to explain, first of all, what happened in that neighbourhood, under what conditions this conversation took place, because this conversation was conducted during fierce fighting, when we had ten -- eight dead and ten wounded on that day, and also eastern Ilidza came under attack from that part as well on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: One moment, Dr. Karadzic. So is the answer to my question "Yes"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is my conversation with an unknown individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two interventions in the transcript. Line 24, page 79. It's unfinished. The witness said that this poetic figure was an issue of loyalty, and then 81, line 5, let us repeat precisely how many people were killed and how many were wounded. I think that the figures in the transcript are wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that can be checked. Back to you, Mr. Tieger. This is a Prosecution witness, and it's your case. I'm not seeking -- the Bench will not seek to determine for the Prosecution how it should proceed, but if the witness is not satisfied with the accuracy of the transcript, then it's of less weight and value in due course to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I will not go through this exercise with every intercept, but in this particular case, let's play it. Do the interpreters have the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: There's an alternative, of course. What could happen is that we could move on to another topic, but in the adjournment, which is inevitable and going to start in about 25 minutes, the witness could compare the transcript with the tape himself, as could somebody from the Office of the Prosecution. If there's unanimity, then there's no issue. If there is an issue, then the issues can be tested in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to -- if it's possible to play this now, I'd like to do it. I think the witness is going to assist on that in any event. I would like to move past this issue, get on to the remainder of the examination and conclude it. I hadn't -- I had hoped it wouldn't be this long. This seems, probably for understandable reasons, to be a focus of the witness and I'd like to get out of the way. But let's see if we can get a transcript to the interpreters as soon as possible. That will take a couple minutes. I'll move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I intervene?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: If it's going to be useful, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, hopefully the majority of my interventions are useful. If we give the transcript to the interpreters, we will achieve nothing, because the witness had an objection to the translation as well. Could we ask the interpreters to interpret this live?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: As I understand it, that's what we're about to embark upon, so that's what Mr. Tieger's intentions are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, do I understand you have a transcript of this conversation in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, why don't you stop us where you say that something significant has been left out of the transcription of that conversation as we listen to it.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the three dots that appear, there will be pretty much of that that is left out, but all right, I will stop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You do that on the basis of the audio. And can you please read out the marking of that transcript that you're looking at, the number. It should have a number at the very top.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: CD76-9-3 over 04 over 026.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is there a number immediately above that to the right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is 0401-3853. It's difficult to see because I have it in handwriting. Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Reid.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Prstojevic: Hello, hello. Good evening. How are you? "UMP: It will be better. "Prstojevic: This is Prstojevic. I need to speak to Mrki. "UMP: Mrki is not here. Mrki 2 is here. "Prstojevic: Give me Mrki 2. "UMP: One moment."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This portion is inaudible, interpreter's note. [Voiceover] "Prstojevic: Good evening. How are you? This is Prstojevic. "Milenko: I am Mika's deputy. "Prstojevic: Yes. What is your name? "Milenko: Milenko. "Prstojevic: Why did Mika call me? "Milenko: He wanted to see about these people in Kotorac, what to do about them. "Prstojevic: Did you arrest them? What did you do? "Milenko: People are down there now. Moment, just a moment. "Prstojevic: Hello? "Milenko: Yes. "Prstojevic: And where are these people? Have they been arrested? "Milenko: No. "Prstojevic: What happened? "Milenko: Down on the road, everything. We have men separated and women are on the road also separated. Just a moment. "Prstojevic: Above ... yes? "Milenko: Men say ... now I just received information that men are in the prison in Kula and women had left towards Butmir."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, this is too fast for a simultaneous interpretation. And sound quality is terrible. [Voiceover] "Novakovic: Women are not in Butmir. "Prstojevic: They cannot go to Butmir. Butmir is going to be mopped up. How about Bascarsija? And put the men in prison. "Novakovic: All right. Then we'll call back to you. "Prstojevic: And as I say, those who convert to Orthodox Christianity can stay, the women and children. "Novakovic: All right. All right. "Prstojevic: But please don't make any mistakes. You did this excellently, which means that Butmir is going to be mopped up with time. Tell those people up there. "Novakovic: All right. "Prstojevic: Good-bye."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Prstojevic, the Court will also have a chance to listen to that audio on its own, to hear the sound of your voice, to hear the response of your interlocutor, but why don't you tell the Court now what your problem with this intercept is.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are words that were left out. However, they do not affect the content significantly, because the interpreters managed to catch what was important. I didn't stop the tape for that reason. There is some problem on the last page, and if you allow me, I will try to check the content of this conversation to the best of my ability, and for that purpose it is necessary to explain what happened in Kotorac on that day and on the night between the 22nd and the 23rd of April, because this is significant for the 300 Muslim residents -- residents of Gornji Kotor. Everything else is a completely different story, and the witnesses will contribute to establishing precisely the -- the facts who appear in the court in Sarajevo. On the 21st, when the first all-out attack on Ilidza took place, which was the first ordered attack on a Serbian village, according to the Muslim information we had 11 dead and 56 wounded. However, it was also ordered that this village where there were 300 residents --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I gave you an opportunity to explain what you wanted to explain which was what was left out in this intercept, according to you. Now you verified the intercept, and you embarked on your explanation of its -- the entirety of its backdrop, and that was not what you asked to do originally, and that's not what I'm asking you to do now, but I do have some questions about this, first of all. So with respect to what we heard from the interpreters and what I understand you to have affirmed, there's a reference to taking them all to Bascarsija on foot. Can you tell the Court, please, where Bascarsija was and what kind of area it was.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I will say that. However, at the point when this conversation took place, the entire civilian population was already, for several hours, from 14.30 until 1900 hours, when I was approximately having this conversation, this entire population was in Dobrinja 1 or in Butmir. Bascarsija is, if you take the roundabout road through deep Serbian territory, about ten kilometres away. That is a centre where there are certain craftsmen and where there are shops. It symbolises the Muslim Sarajevo under Muslim control. In this case of Dobrinja 1, it is 300 metres away from us. That is where imprisoned soldiers and civilians were. And as for the other case, those who went to Butmir, that is only 700 metres away. I ask you kindly, Mr. Tieger, in line 4, I say, "Good evening." And then in the other two penultimate lines I say "good evening" twice. I ran in after combat, because we had 8 killed and 50 wounded. You have that there. And I saw that someone called me, code-name unknown. I left my rifle there and I started talking. To this day, I think -- well, this is the telephone of the public security station of Kula and all of this was happening before the public security station of Kula. I think that someone for some reason coded this and looked for cover from me for something that had already been done. I'm not trying to evade anything. Who carried out an armed attack took part in combat and therefore had to take the consequences as well. Now, people with weapons, who were operating with weapons, well, women, children, and many of those who were military conscripts but who actually drove luxury passenger cars or tractors, went wherever they wanted to and no one searched them, but some military conscripts, I don't know how many of them there were, at any rate there were less than 20 of them, they were kept in prison for ten days, and then they were released -- or, rather, exchanged without any further court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, the Court's time is limited. I'm going to move on to another intercept. I'd like to move on to P1492, please. Mr. Prstojevic, this is an intercept that is dated the 14th of June, 1992, and again it's one you not only had an opportunity to listen to more than once but also comment on in court. And it's a conversation between you and a certain Radomir, and then Dragan, and identified there apparently as Dragan Despotovic. First of all, just looking at it quickly, do you remember this was raised during the course of the Krajisnik case, and do you remember this, the discussion about this intercepted conversation?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was shown in Mr. Krajisnik's case, but I've said that generally I do not remember any conversations, but I'm interpreting this and trying to place it in time. I said no one was killed, no one was wounded, whereas there will be some Muslims staying on. Two will get killed only in June, but we are going to have the greatest number of casualties among the civilian population in any local commune, 39, because this was a zone of incessant combat between the two sides, the Serbs and the Muslims. And everybody escaped from there, and those who did not manage to escape got killed, those 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me take you to a few portions of this conversation quickly and elicit some comments before our time concludes for today. So if we can turn to the second page. You asked Dragan the question: "But tell me, did they disconnect all the phones of the Turks in Kasindol?" He says: "Sorry?" You say: "Did they disconnect the phones in Kasindol." And Dragan says: "All the phones are getting disconnected." You say: "They are getting disconnected?" Dragan says: "Everybody's." And you ask: "Had they been disconnected before?" And he said: "Well, theirs had been disconnected before." Now the conversation continues on the next page, and you say: "But tell me this, please." Dragan says: "Yes?" "Well, what shall we do? Would it be good if we gave it a thought and if we organised people from a side or outside to expel them all. Nobody needs to be shot or killed, everybody expelled." And Dragan says: "That would be the right move." And you say: "That is a bit -- let's say that you make preparations. I have a decision from before." Dragan says: "Well, we tried it once but then there were some guardians and it remained that way." And you say: "Well, you cannot. No, they won't -- he will -- let him come if the people are still standing. When they arrive, they will go to hell. He will go with them too." Dragan says: "Agreed." And you say: "Up to Bascarsija." Now, first of all, Mr. Prstojevic, I take it that in this conversation you're referring to the same Bascarsija you were referring to before.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This symbolises the Muslim part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you refer to organising people from outside to expel them all, who did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, this conversation is taking place during the July offensive of the Muslims, and you did not read this out here, that that neighbourhood -- I mean, I am from that neighbourhood. That is the last one before Trnovo. Sparsely populated. It was attacked from the inside and the outside. You did not say that the artillery was hitting very precisely. I am talking to a man here who was are involved in Red Cross-like activity. He was not able-bodied for military service. You see, there are only 1.005 Muslims out of a total population of 1.703. That is to say --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I intervene?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: No, not at this point, Dr. Karadzic. Mr. Witness, do you have a short and affirmative or a short answer, in any event, to Mr. Tieger's question? Regardless of the surrounding circumstances, who did you mean by people from outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is well known who these people are in such a situation, when a place is jeopardised and when its territory can fall. That is to say, the MUP and the military police come out, run out, and they arrest all those who are military age, even if they're Serbian, and if they are escaping from the area. And if there is a fifth column involved, then they have to search premises and check who it is that is firing from this fifth column and who is guiding the artillery, because this is Kotlina. Somebody had to guide the artillery and correct fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The question that Mr. Tieger asked was in relation to this: "Would it be good if we gave it a thought if we organised people from outside to expel them all?" Are you then saying in your answer that what you meant was that the MUP and the military police should be the people to expel them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the MUP from the western part of Ilidza and the military police, but, Your Honour, these people never moved out. Out of these 25 households I know at least five households that remained with us throughout the war. One of the houses is 200 metres away from my house, and they live there to this day. That is to say, we did not do that because the offensive was over. There was no need any longer and nothing was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I will make this, if I may, Your Honour, the last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, you said: "Well, it is well known who these people are in such a situation, when a place is jeopardised ..." You were asked about this --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And now I am impeaching or refreshing, take it any way, and I think I have the Court's permission, I trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were asked in 2005 about this very conversation, and at page 41, you were asked: "When you say 'bring people from outside,' who are you thinking of?" That's page 41 of the English and in the B/C/S page 77. And your answer was: "For example, I think about the group of Arkan's, group of Boban, Brne's group who was from Pale, any unit from outside." That's what you said, isn't it, Mr. Prstojevic, and that's what you meant by "people from outside."

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. I am going to review that after this, or I'm asking for a break straight away so that I review it. I did not say that. You are totally deluded, Mr. Tieger. You will see I have all the answers that I provided. It's in this documentation that I have in my briefcase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, how much longer in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we continued at the same rate, of course it would be a considerable time. I am going to review both this transcript, the -- consider the witness's positions, and I can assure the Court I will endeavour to reduce the remainder of the examination-in-chief to a minimum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I am simply thinking -- I'm principally thinking of the witness that is fixed for next week, whether or not there might be a necessity to interpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I -- well, I'm sure in light of the length of cross-examination that has been allocated that will -- and I appreciate that the Court was going to review that. I will certainly stick to my previous estimate which leaves me with only a relatively limited amount of remaining time, but I still don't -- unless the Court adjusts the allocation of cross-examination time in a manner I didn't anticipate, then I think the witness -- the fixed witness would intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it. We will rise now, and we will --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say a word?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Again, if it's -- if it's substantially useful, yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm afraid that correcting the transcript will go to the detriment of my time for cross-examination, and I found many mistakes. For example, it's not the July -- the July offensive but it's the June offensive, and it's not 1.005 or 105. So it -- and the Serbs are a majority. So this significantly changes the essence. And I'm afraid that I'm going to spend a considerable amount of time in correcting these transcripts, because they are being selectively presented, which is Mr. Tieger's right, but I really am afraid that I'm not going to have enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, we'll cross that bridge when we get to it, which is always the best thing to do. We'll now rise, and we will sit again at 9.00 on Tuesday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of March, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.34 p.m.,
